summary.title: <antirez>
summary.one_liner: Antirez draws parallels between writing a novel and programming big systems, arguing that rewriting the initial core of a system repeatedly leads to a better design.
takeaways: Good programs and good novels both need well-made local parts and a sound global structure.
Novels are mostly fixed once published, while code is changed continually, which changes how each is written.
Writing prose is largely rewriting; the author suggests programmers should treat the first core of a system as their only bullet and rewrite it repeatedly.
A well-structured initial design tends to shape how a system grows over the years.
Consistent daily work, not occasional bursts, drives progress in both programming and writing.
summary.summary: This is a personal blog post by antirez, written a year after he paused programming to write a science-fiction novel. He argues that programming large systems and writing novels share structural traits, such as needing good local and global elements, consistent daily effort, and dealing with writer's block. The main difference he sees is that novels are essentially immutable once published while code keeps changing. He concludes that programmers should rewrite the initial core of a system many times during its genesis, since that early design strongly shapes later growth. The post ends with a short update on the novel's editing and translation plans.
